alt: A schematic line shows the number of divorces since 1945: a brief post-war rise, a low level in the 1950s and 1960s, a sharp rise after the Divorce Reform Act came into force in 1971, growth to a peak in the early 1990s, then a general fall. Laws are marked: legal aid 1949, 1971, 1984 and no-fault divorce from 2022.
caption: Divorce rose sharply after 1971, peaked in the early 1990s, then fell: not a steady rise.

alt: Three cards. The number of divorces can fall while the divorce rate stays high. Divorce figures miss separations and cohabiting break-ups, so they underestimate breakdown. A rise after a new law may be a backlog of couples already separated. Below: trend, two figures, exception, explanation.
caption: Check what the figures count before you explain them.

after: ## Reasons for the rise in divorce since 1945
alt: Top: four laws made divorce possible, easier, cheaper and quicker: legal aid in 1949, irretrievable breakdown from 1971, applying after one year from 1984 and no-fault divorce from 2022. Below: three social changes made people want divorce: less stigma and higher expectations, secularisation, and women’s changed status.
caption: Laws open the door; changes in attitudes, religion and women’s status explain why people walk through it.

after: ## Reasons for the rise in divorce since 1945
alt: A chain: paid work gives women their own income, so they are less dependent on a husband, leaving becomes realistic, and most divorce petitions are brought by wives. Below, equality laws, welfare benefits for lone parents and feminism also strengthened women’s position.
caption: Independence makes leaving an unhappy marriage a realistic option for women.

alt: Four cards. Husband and wife face financial and emotional costs, but also relief, and many form new partnerships. Children may move, see less of one parent and gain step-families, though conflict may harm more than divorce. The extended family loses or gains contact. Family structures change, with more lone parent families at higher risk of poverty.
caption: Divorce affects every family member and reshapes family structures, not always for the worse.
